title: Investigation of the clinical and analytical performance of two point of care testing devices for the measurement of cardiac troponin I (high sensitivity)
official: Investigation of the Clinical and Analytical Performance of Two point of care testing devices for the measurement of CardiAc Troponin I (high sensitivity): CAPT-CAT
summary:
Background and study aims
Chest pain is one of the most common reasons for attending an emergency department. When someone may be having a heart attack, doctors use a blood test called troponin to look for signs of damage to the heart muscle. Troponin tests are usually performed in hospital laboratories and results can take several hours to become available. New point-of-care testing devices can measure troponin close to the patient and provide results much more quickly. Before these devices can be used routinely in healthcare settings, it is important to establish whether they provide results that are as accurate and reliable as standard laboratory tests. This study aims to evaluate the analytical and clinical performance of two point-of-care high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I devices, Quidel TriageTrue® and Abbott iSTAT®, and assess whether they may be suitable for use in community and acute care settings.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years and over who attend the Royal Glamorgan Hospital with symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome (such as chest pain), who present more than one hour after symptom onset and are able to provide informed consent.

What does the study involve?
Participants who agree to take part will provide additional blood samples at the same time as their routine clinical blood tests. These samples will be tested using the Quidel TriageTrue® and Abbott iSTAT® point-of-care devices. The results will be compared with those obtained using established laboratory-based high-sensitivity troponin tests currently used in Wales. Researchers will assess how accurately the devices identify patients who may or may not be having a heart attack. Laboratory studies will also be conducted using anonymised patient samples to evaluate technical performance measures, including precision, accuracy, linearity, limits of detection and limits of quantification. Healthcare staff will complete questionnaires to assess device usability and suitability for implementation in community healthcare settings.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants are unlikely to receive a direct medical benefit from taking part. However, the results may help improve future assessment of patients with suspected heart attacks by supporting the development of rapid testing closer to the point of care. Risks are expected to be minimal and relate mainly to the collection of additional blood samples, which may cause temporary discomfort, bruising or minor bleeding.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board, Wales, UK, and participant recruitment takes place at the Royal Glamorgan Hospital, Pontyclun, Wales.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to February 2027.

Who is funding the study?
Health Education and Innovation Wales (HEIW).

Who is the main contact?
Professor John Geen, Royal Glamorgan Hospital, john.geen@wales.nhs.uk.
conditions: Patients at the emergency department with chest pain at least 1 hour after the onset of chest pain and soon after arrival at the acute care clinical setting
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Age 18 or over 
2.	Patient has presented with symptoms of an acute coronary syndrome and are being investigated as suspected ACS
3.	Patients has presented more than 1 hour post onset of symptoms
4.	Able to provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Patient has another medical condition (apart from ACS) that would necessitate hospital admission (e.g. sepsis)
2.	Patient lacks mental capacity to provide informed consent
3.	Patients with life-threatening emergencies
4.	Traumatic injury
5.	Not being investigated for ACS
